newsitem.title: FRANCE: Compaq aims to be in the world computer top three.
newsitem.headline: Compaq aims to be in the world computer top three.

text.p: The U.S. Compaq Computer Corporation, the world's number five computer group, aims to surpass "at least" two rivals and be among the top three at the turn of the century, chairman Eckhard Pfeiffer told a news conference on Monday.

"The peaceful revolution of 1996 will be as profound as in 1991, but now we are doing it from a position of strength while in 1991 we were facing a crisis," Pfeiffer, also chief executive officer, said at the first of a series of conferences in Europe.
For now, Compaq has a world lead in the personal computer market, but in the global computer industry it ranks behind IBM Corp, Fujitsu, Hewlett-Packard and NEC.

Its recent results, a 14 percent rise in 1996 second quarter sales to $4.0 billion and a nine percent increase in net income to $267 million, were above the industry average and Pfeiffer expected this to continue.
"We are planning to grow again substantially faster than the overall market," he said. The market is forecast to grow between 17 and 19 percent in 1996, or to 70 million personal computers.
This growth rate is lower then the rise of more than 20 percent in 1995.

Among factors driving the market, Pfeiffer mentioned the start of an era of personal communications -- the combination of computers and telephones -- the upgrade cycle to Intel-made powerful Pentium microprocessors and the newly launched Microsoft Windows NT 4.0 network software which he called "long awaited by the business user".
Ongoing price reductions for the consumers and the development of the Internet and Intranet computer networks is also boosting the market.
"If you're not on the Net then you're out," he said.

The "peaceful revolution" of Pfeiffer, who joined Compaq 13 years ago to head its European operations from Switzerland, is partly a new corporate structure centred on three groups -- Enterprise Computing, Consumer Products and PC Products.
It also aims to reduce costs further and improve lead times and quality to obtain customer loyalty and reduce the total costs of ownership of a computer or system.
The project, codenamed Cross Roads, also has a focus on new markets for Compaq such as small and medium-sized businesses, Internet solutions and Enterprise solutions.
As an example of new products, Pfeiffer said Compaq would start shipping Pentium-powered workstations for Windows NT 4.0 in two months' time.

In Europe, Compaq has a leading position on most of its markets with a 27.2 percent market share in the server market, a 14.4 percent number two place in portable computers, a 12.4 percent share in the business personal computer market and nine percent in consumer personal computers.
Andreas Barth, managing director for Compaq's Europe Middle East and Africa (EMEA) division, said the group aimed to reclaim the number one position in portables -- from Toshiba -- in 1997.
Barth said that the West European micro-computer market was expected to grow by 11 percent in 1996 and accelerate to 15 percent in 1997.

While the rate of growth fell in the last six quarters from 29.4 percent in the first quarter of 1995 to 6.8 percent in the second quarter of 1996, Compaq sees a rise of eight and 14 percent in the next two 1996 quarters and stabilisation at around 15 percent in the next three quarters.
